en: *Yuanjue chao bian yiwu*, Scroll One (with Preface), composed by Guanfu.

Zhiran of Yushi notes that this commentary contains many errors and uncertainties because it was not the work of a single hand, Guifeng Zongmi alone, when it was briefly excerpted from the *Da shuchao*.

Consequently, the disciples collectively abridged and excerpted [the text], resulting in a lack of mutual consistency between the preceding and following sections of the Great Commentary and its sub-commentary (*śāstra*).
Furthermore, through errors in transcription and omissions, as well as alterations made during the carving of printing blocks, Master Qi himself remarked: "I have excised without excising;
this is to return to the original. How much more so when those who removed the original blocks arbitrarily added emendations, leading to successive corruptions that further distorted the text.

As for its source, commentators have failed to realize it; they all claim it is Guifeng’s original text. Some, perceiving its errors, merely add embellishments, resulting in a failure to achieve the intended mark (the *hu*) while adding legs to a snake.
Now, I shall sequentially cite the *Great Commentary* (*Dajie*) and the *Sub-commentary* (*Chao*) for comparison and provide a correct interpretation to distinguish the truth.

If you wish to carve this into printing blocks for circulation, you should revise the various passages based on these details; thus, [the original] Guifeng... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
The heart-lamp of Master Feng illuminates the infinite. Written on the fifteenth day of the tenth month of the Bingyin year of the Xiangshi era by Fangwen of Huayan, Pilin.
Volume One. Ten Sites.
The main text says, "Below this, it is annotated that this explains the character *qian* (乾). Why, then, does it suddenly say so in the annotation?

Furthermore, within this very section, it immediately annotates, "The explanation of the character *qian* is finished. How could one possibly mark the beginning of an explanation and then conclude it by saying it is finished?
However, this commentary also exists in the *Lüchāo* (Abridged Extract) of the ancient edition. Yet, the Qi masters failed to provide corroborating evidence for it; why, then, was it not excised?
Moreover, the *Dàchāo* (Great Extract) lacks this commentary regarding the character "gān" (乾). [As stated in the text: "The evaluation says:

According to what was said above—that one wishes to manifest the four virtues and thus first manifests the Way of Qian—everything from here on is an explanation. Regarding 'The Origin is the eldest of the good,' the commentary cites the *Zhuāngzǐ*."

Regarding the term "yun" (云): it should have been written as "Zhuangshi" (莊氏). Consequently, in the commentary below the character "zhen" (貞), it immediately states "Zhuangshi," and the *Dàchão* consistently uses "Zhuangshi.
This refers to the person who explained the *Yījīng*. If one were to say "Zhuangzi" (莊子), it would conflate him with the book *Zhuangzi*.
Furthermore, the designations used by Master Qi differ before and after; he previously says "Zhuangzi" and later says "Zhuangshi"—this should not be so. This is an error of Master Qi.
This is correct.

Regarding the phrase "the four inversions of flourishing and withering," the sub-commentary notes that this terminology of "withering and flourishing" was established by Tiantai and appears in a separately translated scripture.

However, according to the sub-commentary to the *Dàchāo*, it states: "Regarding the doctrine of withering and flourishing, one finds no such text in the scriptures; it is perhaps the Master’s own interpretation."

[The text] says: "Or it may be a separately translated or separately circulated version of the sutra. If this were the case, one should not now definitively state that the passage exists within a separately translated scripture;
such a claim was merely made in a cursory manner at the time of compiling this *Yao* (Excerpts). Furthermore, according to Qingliang’s commentary on Zhiyi’s interpretation, he states:

"The presence of both withering and flourishing already manifests permanence and so forth. This may be sought through its meaning, or there may be a separate textual basis for it. According to Sengliang, [he says]: "The tree is tall..."

It was about five *zhang* in height; its upper part was joined while its lower part was detached. Its flowers were exceedingly white, and its fruit resembled a jar, possessing both fragrance and flavor.

Now, two trees are flourishing while two trees are withered. This clarifies that the Dharma does not extend everywhere. The commentary states: Although the specific source remains unknown, the principle is quite evident.
Evaluating this, we see that Qingliang cites both Zhiyi and Sengliang, both of whom spoke of such "withering and flourishing."

It further states that it is unknown upon what this is based; moreover, since the *Dàchāo* (Great Commentary) provides the same commentary as Qīngliáng, one should know that it is improper to categorically conclude that it is a separately translated version.

Under the passage "Concentrating the vital energy to achieve suppleness," the commentary mentions "Héshànggōng and others," yet this commentarial remark does not appear in the *Dàchāo*; however, [the following]...
Furthermore, the footnote states that all such notes are individual commentaries by the same author;

moreover, since there are annotations both above and below this passage, and these are all the words of Master Heshang Gong, why is it that this particular section alone is singled out [as being different], thereby making the preceding and following sections appear as if they were not the words of Master Heshang Gong? This must surely be incorrect.
This subsequent addition by the Qi masters is truly strange.
The statement that "the mind directs the vital energy (*qi*)" is explained in the sub-commentary as follows:

"If one relies on the *Da chao* and the ancient *Lüechao*, both state that the mind should be single-mindedly focused to achieve harmony and gentleness, so that while the spirit and energy are truly internal, the physical form remains weak and supple. If the vital energy were allowed to act arbitrarily..."
If one acts in such a way, the harmonious breath departs from within, yet the physical form remains rigid and strong; this is a failure.
Examining the original commentary of Master He Shang, it is also identical to the version of Qi Shi. Why not base oneself on the original text and instead make arbitrary alterations?

Since these have been changed, they are no longer the original commentary; consequently, the concluding note at the end—which states that each is the language of the respective commentary—becomes untenable.
[This is] obscure. The *Śāstra* (Jikong Chao) explains that "arising through the conjunction of conditions" means there are four kinds of conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*), and so forth;

it then proceeds to explain them specifically in terms of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and so forth. [The author] critiques this, saying: "In this context, the original comparison has been lost. Nevertheless, among the four conditions, the causal condition is the direct cause."

The three conditions, such as the augmenting condition (*upaniṣad-pratyaya*) and so forth, are remote conditions (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). It is only when these four conditions are complete that they constitute the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the arising of dependent origination from multiple factors.

Now, although four [types of] conditions have been enumerated, the statement "speaking here specifically in terms of causal conditions" refers to explaining the meaning of internal and external dependent origination by combining the causal conditions among those four.
Although this combines them within the *Śū* (the *Śāstra*), it contradicts the listing of the four conditions in the *Chao* (the *Vyākhyā*).
As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle 7: "Regarding dependent origination through discrimination, how should one understand the characteristics of this dependent origination?

There are four conditions (*pratyaya*)... (and so forth; these are the four conditions). Therefore, Qingliang [Xuanzang] explains that within internal conditions, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in relation to grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) in relation to birth (*jāti*), possess the meaning of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This is because among the four [conditions], craving is the increase of grasping, and becoming is the increase of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Thus, this...

Because the *nidāna* (causal condition) must directly produce the essence of the fruit, only the four links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), and birth (*jāti*) are said to possess the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The remaining eight links are explained in terms of the other three conditions. Thus, one should know that the twelve links of dependent origination fully embody the meaning of the four conditions;

only then are they the causal conditions of dependent arising. If one first lists the four conditions and then says, "for now, we shall explain them according to the causal condition," it is because...

To fail to distinguish between the general and the specific is a flaw in the presentation of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa). One should eliminate the "four conditions" and simply state that existence arises from the convergence of conditions, whether internal or external; only then will it be correct.

The Commentary states: "Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream. (In both the *Da shu* and *Xiao shu*, the character for "affliction" [患] in "patient affliction" [病患] has been erroneously used for the character for "transformation" [幻] in "illusory transformation" [幻化]. The *Dà cǎo* manuscript reads "patient affliction.")

However, the *Xiǎochāo* (Small Commentary) erroneously uses the character "huàn" (illusion/magical transformation). This is certainly a scribal error. Currently, all eight instances of the character "huàn" throughout the *Xiǎochāo* are incorrect.
Later, when the text was carved for printing, the *Dàchāo* (Large Commentary) was also consulted for comparison; it was recognized that the correct character should be "bìng" (affliction/sickness).
Yet, in the *Dàshū* (Large Commentary), the character "huàn" remains unchanged, which results in a contradiction between the *Shū* and the *Chāo*. Now, fearing this...

This passage is difficult to believe; let us examine it together. First, since the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary) states that the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) system also contains this [teaching], and further states that "among the two metaphors, for now we rely on the dream," yet after finishing the explanation of the dream, it says:

"If one explains by relying on the metaphor of the illness" (*shì yuè bìng-zhàng zhī yù shuō zhě*)—this is a citation of the second metaphor concerning illness, as explained at length in the *Chao*. Since both the *Chao* and the *Shu* (the Commentary) employ the term "illusory transformation" (*huàn-huà*), why does [the text] suddenly cite "illness"?

If you say that the "suffering" [in the term *byō-tan*] is released from its "suffering," yet you do not explain it in terms of being like an illusion or a transformation (*māyā-nirmāṇa*), then what is this?

If one were to explain the "illusion" of an illusion or transformation by means of the "suffering" of illness, then the character for "suffering" (*byō*) would lack its intended force. Consider this. However, one might fear that a skeptic would object:
"What prevents us from explaining it as 'illusion' or 'transformation'? For in the *Chō* (the *Shōdaijōron Ryakusho*), it is explained in terms of refuting the Vijñaptimātra school."
To explain it by using the character "huàn" (sickness) is fundamentally incorrect. The original text refers to *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), as cited in the *Chao*.
Furthermore, the *Da chao* (Great Commentary), fascicle 12, clarifies that it cites the character "huàn" from that treatise and provides an extensive explanation based on the tenets of that school.

Yet, the *Da shu* (Great Sub-commentary), fascicle 3, instead uses the characters "huàn-huà" (illusion-transformation) and "bìng-huàn" (sickness). This, too, is an error in the sub-commentary; therefore, the present *Chao* [corrects it].
The text does not clarify which characters were used; it simply states, "All is consciousness alone, and consciousness is like one suffering from a dream," citing the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

(In the present manuscript, this was also erroneously written as "illusion" [幻化]; since the original text correctly uses the character for "sickness" [患], I have now adopted that reading. Thus, it says, "I now employ that text."

It is certain beyond doubt that the *Shuchao* (Commentary on the Commentary) must employ the character "huàn" (affliction/illness). [The twelfth fascicle of the *Chao* discusses how the visual faculty is impaired by affliction, such that one sees blue, yellow, and so forth, or various persons and objects.

The *Yuanren lun* (Treatise on the Original Person) also uses that same passage, stating: "In a severe illness, the mind is clouded and one sees strange colors, persons, and objects. However, the present *Chao* refers to the specific case of "hot cataracts," whereby one sees floating flowers and the like. Nevertheless, using the meaning of the character "huàn," it is appropriate for all such explanations.

The *Chao* herein correctly presents the contemplation of "extinguishing and transcending all attachments" (*minjue wuji guan*). This has been verified against ancient manuscripts and the Yuan edition of Master Qi.

The original text and the Great Commentary (Daishu) are both identical. However, later individuals, seeing that the subsequent passage also says "that [text] also says" and so forth—which is the text concerning the contemplation of "reducing form to emptiness"—failed to understand the intent of the Sub-commentary (Shō).
Acting on their own whims, they used the printing blocks to erase the four characters "泯絕無寄" (minketsu mujū) and changed them to "會色歸空" (esoku kikū).
Unaware of their own delusion, they have dared to make such a bold alteration to the woodblocks.
This is indeed strange. I shall now explain it for you. The *Chao* states: "In the midst of this, it is precisely the contemplation of total cessation and non-reliance.

This sentence points directly to the core meaning. That text also says that the subsequent phrase does not explain the meaning of "precisely the correct state," because it refers to the contemplation of the convergence of form into emptiness, wherein both are empty and there is no form.
Since the present case likewise transcends even emptiness, that passage is cited as a comparison.
What is being selected here is precisely the state of perfect correctness, where all things are extinguished and there is nowhere to rely.

However, when the *Dachao* (Great Commentary) cited this passage on "returning form to emptiness," it was originally intended to prove the convergence of the delusive to reveal the true, employing the method of subsuming phenomena by means of principle (*li*).

It was only later, when the *Luechao* (Abridged Commentary) was compiled, that the passage was moved to its current position, thereby conversely clarifying the meaning of perfect correctness, where all things are extinguished and there is nowhere to rely.

Furthermore, from the latter part of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* down to the passage "therefore he is called the Bodhisattva Sāgaramudrā," it is likewise stated: "This is called the Bodhisattva’s Sāgaramudrā Samādhi.
This is consistent with both the *Lüchāo* (Brief Extract) of the Old Edition and the *Dàchāo* (Great Extract). This is the actual text of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*;

however, the masters of the Qi dynasty saw only the section on the "Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva*), which states: "It universally seals all mental activities; therefore, perfect enlightenment is named 'Non-existence' (*Anupalabdhi*)."
[The character] "liàng" (量) was hastily changed to "pútí" (菩提). This is all the more evident since the *Xianshou pin shu* (Commentary on the "Chapter on the Wise Leader") also cites it quite clearly.
Yet, how could Master Xi, who has already collated and verified this minor detail, have been equally deluded? Regarding the sectioning [of the text]:

"Comparing it to the Sea-Seal [Samādhi], surpassing that Great Void as a metaphor"—in reality, the upper clause uses a metaphor to illustrate the Dharma, while the lower clause uses the Dharma to clarify and distinguish; yet both are categorized [as such].
What is the analogy of the cloud?
In the second fascicle, the *Shichu Chao* states:
"Because one contemplates and practices [the teaching] (taking the capacity of those to be converted as the object), it is called wisdom" (and so forth). The *Da Chao* is likewise.

The commentary states: "This is because the treatise discusses the causal conditions for the practice of contemplation (*cintāmayī-pratipatti*). Qingliang’s (Chengguan) explanation says: "The 'cause' (*hetu*) refers to the wisdom of the teacher;

the 'condition' (*pratyaya*) refers to the capacities of those to be converted. Because one intends to employ the sublime Dharma attained to suit the capacities of beings, it is called the 'practice of contemplation.
According to this, the character 'practice' (*xing*) should logically be placed above the character 'cause' (*yin*), yet it remains below the character 'practice'."

The commentary states that "the wisdom capable of teaching" refers to the [wisdom] that takes the characters as its object; below the word "characters," it notes "the capacities of those to be transformed.

This is precisely the text from the *Qīngliáng* (Cool Grove). Alternatively, one might simply move the four characters "capacities of those to be transformed" to appear under the words "conditioned practice" (*yuánxíng*), so that it would read "causal practice and conditioned practice.
This is also the intended meaning of the treatise. The fact that this note is not placed in its proper location is likely a scribal error.
The *Chao* (Commentary) explains that emptiness and existence manifest alternately, stating: "Either first or later, they are simultaneous and mutually opposed," and so forth.
In the explanation, regarding the first period of teaching, it is held that mind and object both exist; in the second period, both mind and object are empty. The note states:

"In the former two, there is alternation between priority and posteriority. In the third period, the object is empty while the mind exists. The note states: "There is simultaneity and mutual opposition. Now...
Regarding the detailed meaning of mutual interdependence (*anyonya-apekṣā*): it must be that emptiness comes first and existence comes later, or existence comes first and emptiness comes later;

or else, existence and emptiness must occur simultaneously, such that when the object is empty the mind exists and when the object exists the mind is empty. Only then can the sense of mutual interdependence be established across these sequences of before, after, or simultaneity.

However, in the first moment there is only the existence of the mind and the object, while in the second moment there is only the emptiness of the mind and the object; this merely constitutes "existence preceding emptiness."

Furthermore, "subsequent" does not carry the meaning of mutual succession. Moreover, if in the third period the object is empty while the mind exists, then one emptiness and one existence would be simultaneous;

thus, there too would be no sense of mutual succession. Observe that the explanatory notes appended to these two sections must have been arbitrarily added by later generations and do not reflect the intention of Master Guishan;
it would be excellent to excise them. The original intent of the *Chao* (Excerpts) is merely to provide a general explanation of "emptiness" among the ten pairs.
Because there are cases of priority, posteriority, and simultaneity occurring reciprocally, the *Chao* concludes by stating:

"The ten pairs of 'emptiness' and 'existence' mentioned above all concern both phenomena (*dharma*) and time; they alternate between being implicit and explicit, which is why it is said they are 'mutually manifest.

Regarding the phrases 'the mind penetrates' and 'phenomena are pervasive,' the ancient editions of the *Chao* as well as the *Da Chao* both state that the meaning of 'the mind penetrates' already includes 'phenomena penetrate,' whereas the meaning of 'phenomena are pervasive' does not include 'the mind.'"
[The term] "pervasive" (biàn) is consistent with the two masters [Hui]qí and [Fǎ]xī; they did not understand the text of the *Chāo* (Excerpts).

Instead, they merely observed the *Shū* (Commentary), which states, "the mind penetrates and phenomena are pervasive," and interpreted this to mean that because the mind contains phenomena, phenomena are pervasive.

Consequently, they only spoke of "the mind penetrating and phenomena being pervasive" (*xīntōng fǎbiàn zhī*), failing to mention "phenomena being pervasive and the mind penetrating" (*fǎbiàn xīntōng*). How much error there is! They did not realize that this was due to...

The four characters cited as scriptural evidence in the *Chao* (Commentary) quote the passage from the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*: "Because the mind is pure, the body, the elements, and so forth are pure.
This refers entirely to the penetration of the mind. Within this, the purity of the body, the elements, and so forth, constitutes the meaning of the penetration of the dharmas contained therein.

Later, it is cited that because the nature of awakening is perfect and boundless, the sense organs, objects, and so forth all pervade the Dharma-realm; this refers to the pervasiveness of phenomena (*dharma*).

Within the text, it is also stated that "because awakening is perfect and boundless, the sense organs and objects are all-pervading. This speaks of the pervasiveness of phenomena and does not include the pervasiveness of the mind.
The commentary provides the reason for this, stating: "The mind is precisely the awakened mind; there is nothing that can be pervasive," and so on. This can be seen through careful reflection.

The *Chao* (Commentary) cites a sutra, saying: "Good son, empty space is thus equal and unmoving, extending downward to eighty-four thousand [yojanas]," and so forth, citing this to establish the pervasiveness of the Dharma (*dharmavyāpti*).
However, this passage does not exist in the *Yuan-chao* (Original Commentary); it merely quotes from the section beginning with "Good son, the nature of awakening (*bodhita*) is all-pervading.
Examining this text now, it neither retreats to the previous point regarding the mind’s universal penetration, nor advances to the subsequent point regarding the pervasiveness of the Dharma.
Therefore, the *Daichao* does not cite this; why then did the Qi masters add it? One should rely on the *Daichao* as authoritative (this passage may also be deleted).

Regarding the phrase "whipping and flogging" (*chāo biān tà zhě*): the *Lüchāo* (Abridged Commentary) reads "whipping and striking" (*biān chuí*); the *Dàchāo* (Great Commentary) states, "it does not trouble [one] to strike.
Why did Master Qi change "striking" (*chuí*) to "flogging" (*yé*)?

The *Chāo* cites the *Lìlì* (Exemplary Cases), stating, "Speech arises from the elephant," with a sub-note below saying, "subsequently, the elephant arises from speech. Below the character "intention" (*yì*), there is a sub-note which says: [text missing].
The *Yìshēng* (Arising from Thought) [commentary] follows after the *Xiàng* (Elephant). Why is it that the *Qíshī* alone is so particularly negligent and erroneous?
Both the *Gǔlüèchão* and the *Dàchão* annotate that the words "arising from the elephant" are clear and distinct in their meaning.

Regarding the statement, "The explanation of this meaning is as previously set forth in the *Benqǐyīn* (Causes and Conditions of the Original Arising)," I have examined the preceding commentary (*chāo*) but do not find such an explanation there.

However, that preceding commentary merely explains the very first mind of the *Benqǐ*, and then refers one to the subsequent sub-commentary (*shū*). Yet, it is actually within that subsequent sub-commentary that it says:
Those who seek the fruit must necessarily examine the cause; if the cause is not true, the fruit will likewise be false.

This refers precisely to such acts as casting images of the Buddha from genuine gold, which is what is indicated here. Although this refers back to the previous *Chao*, even though they are in the same volume, it was overlooked and not cross-referenced;
this too is an original error in the *Da Chao*.
The commentary states that this is from the *Daochao jing*. Although the full text is cited below, when lecturing, it is sufficient to cite only the first two lines.
This annotation was originally made at the time of compiling the *Xiulue chao* (Abridged Commentary). Its underlying intention is to ensure there is no interference;

thus, when lecturing on the entire chapter of the *Guanglüe chao* (Extensive Abridged Commentary), it is not necessary to use what follows. Even though this annotation has been added, it was nonetheless omitted from within this current commentary at that time.

The text following the "Exiting" [section] contains only two phrases. This represents a lapse in illumination for this entire period. If these annotations were to remain, they should be treated like the *Daichao* (Great Commentary), with the subsequent revised text added.
If only those two phrases were retained, they would be useless in the context of the sutra.

The *Chao* (Excerpts) cites the *Niepan yi jue* (Decisions on the Meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra), where the *Da chao* (Great Excerpts) states: "Now, that which arises must perish; having perished, it arises again.

When perishing is itself extinguished, there is no arising; when arising is itself extinguished, there is no perishing. Where there is neither perishing nor arising, this is equal to the cessation and bliss [of nirvāṇa].

In the present *Chao*, the phrase "when perishing is itself extinguished, there is no arising" has been omitted, which renders the meaning unstable and incomplete. This is because these two subsequent phrases serve as the commentary for the two preceding lines of the heading. First...

The first two lines explain the two characters "arising" and "ceasing. The next two lines correctly explain the two characters "having ceased," which refers to the cessation of both arising and ceasing mentioned above.

The final two lines conclude by returning to the point that their simultaneous cessation constitutes bliss. One should not interpret these as explaining the cessation of arising and ceasing separately.

It merely states that "extinction and arising are without extinction. Therefore, one should know that as in the *Dàcǎo* (Great Commentary), by adding "the extinction of extinction is without arising," the meaning becomes stable and lucid;
this [phrase] was simply omitted here.
The *Shu* (Commentary) quotes the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, stating: "Even if one were to wear upon one's crown for kalpas as numerous as dust motes a four-line verse...

According to both the *Huayan Da shu* (Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka) and the *Yanyi* (Exegesis), this is all said to be from the *Sūtra*. However, it remains uncertain which sūtra is being referred to;

while the *Yanyi* simply states that another sūtra is being cited, here it specifically says the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*. Thus, there is doubt regarding these two sources. Furthermore, the *Yanyi* includes another verse: "Only those who transmit and uphold the treasury of the true Dharma..."

Proclaiming the teachings and doctrines to bestow upon all sentient beings, and practicing single-mindedly to accord with True Suchness (Tathatā)—this is precisely what constitutes a true repayment to the Tathāgata.

The *Chao* (Sub-commentary) explains the underlying thread: "Now, the lecturer, having devoted their efforts to memorizing the scriptural text, shall proceed to explain it here. [The *Shu* (Commentary) now...]
This must mean that one should first memorize the commentary (*vyākhyā*) before explaining this sutra; how could there be a principle of memorizing the sutra and then explaining the commentary?
This is certainly a scribal error.
In the preface to his *Shijiao* (Exegesis on the Teachings), where he encountered this scripture, he recorded:

"In the first month of the first year of the Changqing era, I again retired to the Caotang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan to cut off all traces of worldly involvement and cease all external conditions. There, I cultivated my nature and refined my wisdom.

By the spring of the second year, I took the previously composed topical outline (*kewen*) and the two fascicles of the *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium) [and so forth], and following my own humble understanding, I composed a commentary (*shu*). This continued until the summer of the third year."
Only then was the work completed. The remainder is as explained below; the section concerning the "fang" (method/aspect) will be annotated and explained when it arrives later.
It then states that in the second year of the Changqing era, he revised the commentary at Caotang Monastery, finally completing it in the autumn and winter of the third year.

Furthermore, regarding the composition of these various commentaries as the foundation for this present work, the *Shi lüan guàn Huáyán* (Explanation of the Huayan Sutra’s Threads and Flowers) states: "In the [second] year of Changqing..."
In the second year of the Qingyuan era, at Nanshan Fengde Temple, Gunwan and others [compiled this work].

Furthermore, in the summer of the third year of the Changqing era, while listening to the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) at Fengde Temple, they collected the texts of the Vinaya and its commentaries (*shu*) and codified them into three fascicles.

The critique states: According to the preceding account, in the first year of Changqing he secluded himself at Caotang Temple; in the second year he began composing the commentary (*shu*); and in the third...
The work was completed during the summer of that year. Furthermore, it is stated here: "In the second year of the Changqing era, at Fengde Temple;
[the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*] was compiled over three years at Fengde Temple. Because I listened to the former [master], I was entrusted with the Vinaya. This constitutes one contradiction.

Moreover, the various commentaries were composed for the purpose of this present commentary; they should have been composed earlier, yet now they appear to be contemporaneous. Since both... [the text ends].
It is said that he completed the commentary during the summer of the third year, and it is also said that he completed it in the autumn or winter.
From this, we know that at that time he was specifically observing the summer retreat at Caotang Temple.

How could he have been simultaneously residing at Caotang Temple to compose the commentary while also attending lectures on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* at Fengde Temple? Furthermore, for both the second and third years, he remained entirely at Fengde Temple.
The temple provided the resources for the composition of the commentary (*śāstra*). Furthermore, for two or three years, he was entirely at Cōngtáng Temple while composing the commentary.
I do not understand how it is that he records his own dates and place of residence in such a manner that they contradict one another;

this is something that cannot be reconciled, and I can only regard it as a matter of doubt. The *Shū* (Commentary) states that it was transmitted to Qiángxué. The *Chão* (Excerpts) says "already transmitted to Qiángxué," using the character "yǐ" (already).
Both characters are applicable. According to the sequence of the *Chao* (Excerpts), it states: "The *Shu* (Commentary) was completed three years ago;

This phrase, "this self-view," refers to one of the four afflictions within the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*), and so forth. [End of] Evaluation.

It is said: Regarding this passage in the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshū*) and the *Great Sub-commentary* (*Dàchão*), it appears that later generations, failing to understand the Master’s intent, arbitrarily modified the text.

Thus, the *Great Commentary* states: "The latter phrase, 'self-view,' refers to the grasping subject (*nengqǐ*). Since self-view is the faculty of wisdom (*huì*) among the specific mental objects (*biéjìng*), Asaṅga’s *Vajracchedikā-śāstra* treats it as the grasping of phenomena (*fǎqié*).

(This practice assigns self-view to the wisdom that takes objects and correlates it with the grasping of phenomena, rather than correlating it with the self-view within the seventh consciousness. This sub-commentary, conversely, contradicts the *Great Commentary*.)"

It may also be considered that "I" refers to self-delusion (*ātma-moha*) and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), while "those who love me" refers to self-love (*ātma-sneha*) and self-pride (*ātma-māna*).

(The *Dàchāo* [Great Commentary] places the phrase "it may also be considered" below this; Fang states that because there are four afflictions within the seventh consciousness when grasping at a self, the sutra is explained according to this. The *Xiǎochāo* [Small Commentary] likewise should not simply state that these four afflictions exist within this consciousness. Since the previous *Xiǎoshū* [Small Sub-commentary] omitted this meaning, the character "this" (*cǐ*) here merely points to the listing of the four afflictions in the sub-commentary.

It previously stated that the aforementioned view of self belongs to the wisdom of the specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-hetu*) and was not assigned to the seventh consciousness; it is only now that it is assigned to the four afflictions. However, the current *Chāo* [Commentary] does not agree with this.

The preceding "view of self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is assigned as one of the seven consciousnesses. It is explained that the pervasive and clear perception of the self-retribution is designated as "view," because this pervades both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
The *Great Commentary* itself assigns it to the wisdom (*prajñā*) among the specific objects (*viśeṣālambana*) as well as to the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

Moreover, since this is generally discussed in relation to what ordinary beings are deluded about, how could it merely assign the single affliction of the seventh consciousness as the grasping view? Furthermore, the seventh...

The seventh [consciousness] grasps at an internal self and gives rise to views. It is clear that later generations, not understanding this, arbitrarily altered the text to such an extent. This commentary should have stated:

"This phrase, 'self-view,' refers to the wisdom (*prajñā*) within the category of specific objects (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*); therefore, Asaṅga’s *Vajracchedikā-śāstra* considers it to be attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Furthermore, that which is censured as attachment to self (*ātma-grāha*) is the seventh consciousness, because within this consciousness there are four afflictions (*kleśa*). Namely: [the four afflictions are...]
"False appearances, self, self-delusion, self-view, and so forth (etc.). Therefore, the present *Chao* [Commentary] takes [these] from among the four delusions of the seventh consciousness.
The previous attempt to universally correlate them with two phrases of the sutra text was all a later person's arbitrary alteration; it is not the original intent of the *Chao*.

The present intent of the *Chao* lies in explaining the mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*) and refuting the inverted views regarding the true and correct dharmas, thereby providing an explanation. According to the *Da shu* [Great Commentary], there is no refutation.
This was later added by someone who had altered the original woodblock; if it were reversed, it could indeed be refuted, but why would the correct version be refuted? The correct text states:

"To understand the inverted and correct dharmas such as the mental factors (citta-saṃskāra) is what is meant by 'understanding'. The Sūtra is like a hollow sound resonating outward from within a vessel.

The three interpretations in the *Śū* and *Cāo* all miss the original intent of the Sūtra. Furthermore, the *Kuò Shū* says: "The *lóu-jū* bell prevents the resonance from passing through because its physical form obstructs it."

Regarding the sound of the pipes: if the resonance does not penetrate, it is because one is deluded by this commentary, which consequently offers three interpretations. Now, as for the phrase "like the *huang* in a vessel" within the Sūtra:
"vessel" (*qi*) is a general term for musical instruments, while "bell" (*zhong*) is one specific type among such instruments.

However, the *huang* is produced precisely by the sound of the bell, rather than being taken as the physical substance of the bell itself. This is like the performance of music in the *Daya*, where all the various instruments sound forth simultaneously.

At that time, only the sound of the bell was clear and penetrating, emerging beyond the sounds of all the other musical instruments; hence it is said that "the sound of the *huang* [bell-clapper] within a vessel emerges outside.

Because afflictions (*kleśa*) and nirvāṇa do not obstruct one another, and because the combined sounds of all the musical instruments cannot interfere with or obscure the sound of the *huang*, the bell alone emerges. It stands apart from both afflictions and nirvāṇa to signify their ultimate transcendence.
This refers to the "spiritual mind" (*lingxin*). Here, the character *huang* (鍠) is used in its primary sense; it does not carry the meaning of the characters *huang* (鐄) or *huang* (簧).

Thus, we know that Master Ke’s interpretation was slightly inconsistent. However, let us further examine this: since the character *huang* denotes the sound of a bell, and the scripture states "the vessel is resonant" (*qi huang*), the "vessel" (*qi*) takes on the substance of various musical instruments, and by extension, the sound of those instruments as well. The subsequent line states, "the sound issues forth externally. This...
The term "sound" (*śabda*) encompasses the sounds of various musical instruments; however, that which issues forth externally alone is the sound of the bells (*hāṅ*).

As for the other confused and overlapping noises that cannot be distinguished, these are the various musical instruments themselves. Therefore, we know that the metaphor correctly takes the unmixed sound of the multitude as its primary referent, rather than the sound of the bells.
It is not because there is emptiness within the vessel that sound is produced and penetrates outward. For when any object whatsoever is struck, sound issues forth;
why then should it be unique to the bell that its sound issues forth when struck? And why should it be specifically the case that the resonance (*huang*) emanates outward?
If one examines all hollow objects without handles— such as those made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or stone— as well as solid objects,
and finds that they too produce sound when struck, why does this sutra single out the bell?
If it is argued that the sound is perceived because it is loud and reaches far, this is incorrect;
for the scripture merely states that the sound issues forth externally, and does not employ the qualities of "distance" or "loudness" as its metaphor—this can be seen through careful reflection.

Therefore, in Master Kuò’s commentary, the phrase "the sound passes through the obstructed pipe" refers precisely to the fact that the sounds of instruments such as pipes cannot intermingle with the sound of the bell; here, the sound of the bell [remains distinct].
If it were to emerge and penetrate outward, how could this be the case for the *gu* and *gong* bells? Furthermore, why would they produce sounds outside like the *guan* and *sheng* flutes?
Since the *guan* has a hollow tube, does it not produce sound externally? Therefore, both the scripture and the intention of [Hui]kao have failed.
The latter two instances of errors are minor and not distinguished individually.
